recall_prompt: Say how you would find the square root of a complex number — what you compute first and what formula you put it into.
insider_note: Keep the sign on a = −5 all the way through: r + a = 13 − 5 = 8 and r − a = 13 + 5 = 18, which halve to 4 and 9. Then say the sign choice — b = 12 is positive, so both parts take the same sign — and keep the ±.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Find the modulus
steps.margin_note: First mark. a = −5 (negative), b = 12. The square of −5 is +25, so r = √(25 + 144) = 13 — the 5, 12, 13 triple.

recall.must_convey: That a = −5, b = 12 and the modulus r = √(25 + 144) = 13.

steps.why: r is always positive, whatever the sign of a. The negative a matters in the NEXT line, where r + a = 13 − 5 = 8 and r − a = 13 + 5 = 18 — the negative sign is where this question differs from 7 + 24i.
common_mistakes: Taking a = 5, losing the sign that changes the next step.

steps.label: Apply the formula
steps.margin_note: Second mark. b > 0, so the two parts share a sign. r + a = 13 + (−5) = 8 and r − a = 13 − (−5) = 18; halved, 4 and 9.

recall.must_convey: That the formula with r = 13 and a = −5 gives ±(√4 + i√9) = ±(2 + 3i).
accept: use root of r plus a by two plus i root of r minus a by two, that is root four plus i root nine, so plus or minus two plus three i
the square root is plus or minus two plus three i

plus or minus two plus three i, and two plus three i squared is minus five plus twelve i

steps.why: With a negative, r + a is the SMALLER of the two numbers, so the real part of the root is the smaller one (2) and the imaginary part the larger (3). Squaring back is the one-line check that the order is right.
common_mistakes: Computing r + a as 13 + 5 = 18 and getting ±(3 + 2i), which squares to 5 + 12i.
